title: Layers of school improvement activity
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart starts from a striking finding: when his leadership team estimated how much of their time went on the actions in the school improvement plan, the answer was around 5%. Rather than treating that as a failure, he uses it to build a model of what 'getting better' means that accounts for where leaders' attention actually goes. He proposes three layers of improvement activity: 'brilliant basics', the maintenance and gradual refinement of processes that reduces variability between classes and subjects; targeted improvement, the familiar action-planning cycle; and innovation, boundary-pushing work beyond the inspection framework. He argues most leadership time should go on the basics, a smaller share on targeted improvement to avoid initiative fatigue, and the smallest on innovation, with the proportions shifting through phases of the year. The layers interact, with targeted priorities and successful innovations eventually moving down to become habitual. He closes by suggesting leaders allocate responsibility according to colleagues' strengths in each layer as a way of building capacity.
points: Hart's team found only about 5% of leadership time went on school improvement plan actions, prompting a broader model of what improvement work actually consists of.

'Brilliant basics' is framed as improvement of a different kind: reducing variability between classes, year groups and subjects by standardising existing best practice rather than introducing anything new.
Keeping targeted improvement to a deliberately smaller share of time is presented as a defence against initiative fatigue, not a lowering of rigour.
The goal of both targeted improvement and innovation is to migrate down the triangle until they become habitual and demand less working memory from colleagues.
Leaders should match colleagues to layers according to their strengths, so that each layer of improvement has enough people paying attention to it.
quotes: We have a school improvement plan and on it there are actions, timelines etc just like every other. Add the end of a term, we analysed the time we had spent on these actions and I asked the leadership team to express it as a percentage of their time.

There will always be some variability in how different teams and individuals enact these processes. Sometimes the work on brilliant basics required by leaders is to make sure that they actually happen as planned and sometimes it is to make sure that they happen to an agreed standard. Much of this work is getting to know the reality of school life and not assuming that the school that exists in our heads is a true reflection.

We might be triggered into making improvements based on attainment or progress data or we might be triggered into action by inspection recommendations. But this is a narrow lens with which to conceive of school improvement.
A necessarily smaller proportion of our time and attention goes on targeted improvement. This requires a different, but perhaps the most familiar mindset of action planning and implementation.
This is once more an entirely different skillset or way of thinking that, if we’re not careful, can distract from the core business of the school, but if done well, can transform our provision.

Great schools get the basics right, no doubt, and the goal of any targeted improvement activity is to make them habitual. So in this model, any current priorities for improvement eventually need to brilliant basics. The goal is to embed them over time so that they require less and less working memory for colleagues to enact.
Some colleagues might be great at raising the tide and getting the basics embedded across a team. Some might be great at mapping out an action plan and implementing a new idea.
